submissions.findingTextShort: The ISSN position stand supports sodium bicarbonate—not bicarbonate generically—for several high-intensity exercise tasks, with performance effects depending on task and dosing context.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: The 2021 International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand synthesizes human sodium-bicarbonate supplementation evidence and concludes that sodium bicarbonate can improve performance in muscular-endurance and high-intensity exercise contexts, especially tasks lasting roughly 30 seconds to 12 minutes. The intervention identity is sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3); the evidence must not be inherited by a generic bicarbonate-ion profile or unrelated bicarbonate salts. The position stand discusses single-dose protocols in the 0.2 to 0.5 g/kg range, with approximately 0.3 g/kg commonly identified as an effective target, but this research receipt is not a consumer dosing recommendation and does not establish benefit for every sport, task, population, or dosing schedule.
submissions.populationContext: Human exercise-performance literature synthesized in an ISSN position stand, including men and women across multiple high-intensity exercise modalities.
submissions.usageContext: Oral sodium bicarbonate supplementation for high-intensity exercise performance; not generic bicarbonate ion, unrelated bicarbonate salts, or clinical alkalinization therapy.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: A position stand synthesizes heterogeneous studies rather than representing one uniform randomized protocol. Effects vary by exercise task, dose, timing, individual response, and adverse-effect burden.

submissions.findingTextShort: Sodium-bicarbonate exercise protocols commonly produce gastrointestinal adverse effects, and higher single doses can increase their incidence or severity.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: The ISSN position stand identifies bloating, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain as common adverse effects of sodium-bicarbonate supplementation and notes meaningful between-person variability. Higher single doses such as 0.4 to 0.5 g/kg may add adverse-effect burden without clear additional performance benefit versus approximately 0.3 g/kg in many protocols. This supports dose-sensitive gastrointestinal-tolerability framing for sodium bicarbonate; it does not quantify risk for every individual or establish comprehensive safety for chronic use, kidney disease, cardiovascular disease, pregnancy, medication interactions or non-exercise indications.
submissions.populationContext: Participants in human exercise-performance studies of sodium bicarbonate summarized by the ISSN position stand.
submissions.usageContext: Exercise-oriented oral sodium-bicarbonate supplementation across varied protocols.
submissions.safetyContext: Gastrointestinal effects are common enough to materially affect tolerability and sometimes exercise performance; dose and timing are important modifiers.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: The position stand does not establish a universal side-effect incidence or a comprehensive medical contraindication profile across all populations and use cases.
